Lets say you have two completely identical train carts rolling down hill 30 degrees on an identical rail. The only difference is that one cart weighs 10000 lbs more than the other cart.

Would the heavier cart accelerate faster than the lighter cart and would the heavier cart reach a higher max speed than the lighter one?

This one has been bugging me for a while, does anyone know?

If, like physicist often do, you're working in a frictionless vacuum, then both carts would accelerate at the exact same rate. This is essentially the same experiment as dropping two balls of different weights from the leaning tower of Pisa. In fact, whether this is done with a vertical drop or rolling of angled rails doesn't matter. If there is no friction, the acceleration from rolling of a 30° angle is equivalent to a vertical drop, only in weaker gravity (the acceleration will be g*sin(30°), which is exactly 0.5*g). Edit: see here for decomposition of gravitational pull in parallel and perpendicular components.

When there is friction, bot against the air and against the rails, then the heavier cart will go faster. This is probably what intuition is telling you the answer ought to be, because it is what you usually experience. It used to be thought that this is how gravity works: it accelerates objects according to their mass. This theory can be found in the works of, for example, Aristotle. It was only in the time of Galileo and Newton that it was understood that gravity accelerates all masses equally.

"When there is friction, both against the air and against the rails, then the heavier cart will go faster"

When you say faster do you mean both higher top speed and faster acceleration?
It should be both; the lighter cart will be slowed more by the air resistance, and thus have a slower terminal velocity. But it would take a looong hill to get up to those speeds.

Yes. It will accelerate faster and to a higher terminal velocity. Although, there are some (unrealistic) cases where in fact the lighter car might end up going faster. The drag by the air will cause the heavier object to go faster. However, the roll resistance is stronger for the heavier object. So, for trains that are very aerodynamic (so the drag matters little) but have really bad wheels (so the roll resistance is important), the heavier one might go slower. In fact, if you were to do this in a vacuum, but don't ignore the roll resistance, then the heavier one will always be slower.

In fact, an interesting variation on this question would be what happens with varying angles. Let's say both trains are initially on horizontal rails (so obviously they'll remain stationary). Now increase gradually the angle of the rails. At a very small angle, the trains will not start moving yet, because they don't have perfect wheels. The lighter one might well start moving at an inclination angle where the heavier still remains stationary.

tl,dr: stick to frictionless vacua or things become very complicated.

Assuming no air resistance, friction, etc they would accelerate at the same rate with no max speed (other than c, but they'd take forever to accelerate that far).

Air resistance would have a greater (though still negligible) effect on the lighter cart, giving the heavier one an imperceptibly faster acceleration and max speed.

For friction, force of friction is proportional to normal force which is proportional to weight, but since the acceleration is coming from gravity which is also proportional to mass friction would have the same effect for both carts in terms of acceleration.

So air resistance would give a small advantage to the heavier cart, otherwise they would be the same even with friction.

They undergo the same acceleration regardless of the mass. Velocity is dependent only acceleration, and not mass, so barring any other accelerations, they will travel at the same speed. The heavier cart, however, will have greater energy than the lighter one due to the mass.

The heavier cart would accelerate faster. What /u/cassis fails to take into account is the retarding force of friction in the wheels, which is pitted against the sine of the angle of the slope times gravity, aka the force of the cart in the direction of the slope. Since that's much greater in the heavier cart, it will accelerate faster.

Easy thought experiment - imagine two empty carts on a slope, but the wheels are too stiff for either of them to move. Now start filling one with sand. Eventually it will get heavy enough to overcome the stiff wheels and start rolling, leaving the other behind. Same thing.
